claims.text: ALI: tx = thrombectomy/embolectomy, thrombolysis (systemic or catheter-directed) or bypass surg.
claims.quote: Treatment of acute limb ischemia consists of thrombectomy or embolectomy (catheter or surgical), thrombolysis (systemic or catheter-directed), or lower extremity bypass surgery.

claims.text: A fibrinolytic, esp by intra-arterial cath infusion, = most effective for occlusions < 2 wks old w intact motor and sensory funct (a salvageable limb);
claims.quote: A thrombolytic (fibrinolytic) medication, especially when given by intra-arterial catheter infusion, is most effective for patients with acute arterial occlusions of < 2 weeks and intact motor and sensory limb function (ie, a salvageable limb)
Tissue plasminogen activator is most commonly used.

claims.text: Catheter-directed: given @ a rate suited to the pt's size and the extent of thrombosis,
claims.quote: the thrombolytic medication is given at a rate appropriate for the patient’s size and the extent of thrombosis

claims.text: USU for 4–24 hrs depending on ischemia severity and signs of thrombolysis.
claims.quote: Treatment is usually continued for 4 to 24 hours, depending on severity of ischemia and signs of thrombolysis

claims.text: Interactions: other drugs that impair hemostasis raise the bleed risk;
claims.quote: Concomitant use of other drugs that impair hemostasis increases the risk of bleeding.

claims.text: in ACS, GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors are ⍉recommended for pts receiving fibrinolytics.
claims.quote: GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors are not recommended for patients receiving fibrinolytics.
Avoid intramuscular injections. Monitor for bleeding.

claims.text: cholest embolization has been reported, so investigate any new embolic event.
claims.quote: Cholesterol embolism has been reported in patients treated with thrombolytic agents. Investigate cause of any new embolic event and treat appropriately.
